title: Rising richness accounted for 61% of a reconstructed thermal diversity decline at 62 Finnish moth traps
abstract: We rebuilt thermal spread and the printed richness-scaled diversity index from 224,364 species count records at 62 Finnish moth traps in 1993-2022. The same 1,242 trap-years gave annual log trends of -0.00581 for the printed index, -0.00228 for thermal spread, and +0.00706 for richness minus one. The exact log identity assigns 60.8% of the index decline to richness, with a conditional spatial bootstrap interval of 34.8-83.1%. The spread interval was -0.00482 to +0.00027 with spatial block and year cluster uncertainty. Presence-weighted spread declined more quickly; the paired count-minus-presence trend was +0.00307, with interval +0.00162 to +0.00452. At 21 traps with good early and late coverage, the count-weighted spread trend was near zero while the mean temperature score rose. Matched records from the earlier summary release had index scales consistent with the printed richness denominator, but differed in species and processing. This extends a prior equation audit with actual counts. It does not correct all sites in the original study or identify cold-tail loss, climate causation or a cause of the wider tracking gap. Code, aggregate evidence, hashes and external-data rebuild instructions are included.

display.caption: Thermal spread, printed index and richness trends on the same records. Blue intervals allow spatial block and year dependence. Orange intervals resample spatial blocks only. Sensitivity fits use the same spread definition.

citations.reason: We extend its equation audit with species counts and measured richness.
It analyzes mean change in the same species records; we test spread and richness.
Weak climate tracking motivates the search for evidence on ecological processes.
Existing source-supply test informed our choice of a different question.
We test the richness dependence of the printed thermal diversity formula on an overlapping raw-data cohort; we do not correct the full source study.
